content_text: [1/2 @realroseceline] Thoughts on Terry Smith and more I think there’s an even bigger idea hiding beneath Terry Smith’s letter. He says they’ll pay more attention to momentum going forward. Most people stopped there. I don’t think momentum was the cause at all. I think it was simply the symptom. The real story is something far deeper, and it applies to almost every legendary business that has ever existed. For years Terry Smith built his reputation by buying businesses with exceptional returns on capital employed. That philosophy wasn’t wrong. In fact, it was one of the greatest investment frameworks ever created. The mistake wasn’t focusing on ROCE. The mistake was forgetting that high returns and long reinvestment runways are two completely different things. Investors obsess over how much capital a business earns on. Far fewer ask how much capital it still can earn those returns on. That second question is infinitely more important because today’s returns tell you about the past, while tomorrow’s reinvestment opportunities determine the future. Markets don’t pay for history, they pay for what still remains. Imagine two businesses both earning a 35% return on capital. The first can reinvest another $10 billion over the next decade at similar returns. The second can reinvest another $200 billion. They look identical on today’s financial statements, yet economically they are worlds apart. One is approaching saturation, while the other is only beginning its journey. This is why I believe so many investors completely misunderstood Terry Smith’s sales. $NVO didn’t suddenly become a terrible business. $LVMH didn’t suddenly forget how to build one of the greatest luxury franchises ever created. The businesses remained exceptional. What changed was the market’s perception of how much extraordinary opportunity still lay ahead. Every great business is fighting a battle that almost nobody talks about. We obsess over competition, disruption and recessions, yet the biggest long term enemy of many compounders is simply success itself. Every factory built, every country entered, every product launched and every acquisition completed consumes part of tomorrow’s opportunity. Great businesses don’t just create value. They quietly consume their future reinvestment runway one capital allocation decision at a time. The irony is that success eventually becomes its own form of competition. A $1 billion company has many ways to double. A $500 billion company has very few. As businesses grow larger, they aren’t competing against rivals nearly as much as they’re competing against their own size. Mathematics becomes a stronger opponent than competition. This also explains why valuation changes long before earnings do. Investors often wonder why a company still producing record profits can lose half its market value. It’s because markets don’t discount today’s economics, they discount tomorrow’s possibilities. Once investors begin to believe that the opportunity set is shrinking, multiples compress even while the business itself continues performing beautifully. I think there’s another mental model hiding here that almost nobody discusses. Every great business has an inventory of future opportunities. Every time management opens another store, launches another blockbuster drug, enters another geography or acquires another business, they’re not just creating value today. They’re also using up one of tomorrow’s opportunities. Opportunity is a finite resource, and the very best management teams spend it wisely. Perhaps this is why so many legendary compounders eventually slow despite remaining wonderful businesses. They didn’t become poorly managed. They simply became too successful. The first trillion dollar ideas have already been executed, and every future decision must be large enough to move an increasingly enormous business. That’s an extraordinarily difficult standard to meet, regardless of how talented management may be. 1/2👇 --- [2/2 @realroseceline] This is the lesson I took from Terry Smith’s letter. ROCE was never the wrong metric. Quality investing was never the wrong philosophy. Momentum wasn’t the real story either. The missing variable was always the duration of exceptional capital allocation opportunities, because a business earning extraordinary returns for another thirty years is fundamentally different from one earning those same returns for only five. Perhaps the most valuable question an investor can ask isn’t, “What return on capital does this business earn today?” Perhaps it’s, “How much exceptional capital can this business still deploy before the runway disappears?” I suspect that single question explains more about long term stock returns than almost any metric you’ll find in a financial statement. 2/2 🌹
